title: Roll a TripleFlask flat from a lean so its layers match
instruction: Spread the medium in the TripleFlask evenly over its three layers, then leave the flask lying flat in its growth position, imprint up, with both hands off it.
context: Why: multilayer flasks are how research and biomanufacturing labs grow adherent cells past single-flask scale, and each seeding must leave the same volume of suspension on every layer: a layer that gets less grows sparse, one that gets more wastes medium and cells, and the whole flask is harvested at once. The knack: the three compartments share medium through the flask's closed end, so it keeps running down into the lower layers for as long as the flask is being turned flat. The maker's technical note says to rest the flask on its side, hold it at 75 degrees to the work surface, then quickly but gently tilt it into the growth position, imprint up. Rolled straight over from upright, or slowly and carefully, the bottom layer ends too full; landed hard, medium splashes into the neck. Unlike pouring tasks, nothing leaves the vessel: the result is the split inside it. Done by: cell-culture technicians and research associates in academic and biotech labs.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y to the robot's left), heights above the table top. Work surface: the station table, standing for a biosafety cabinet's stainless steel work surface. Flask: a Thermo Scientific Nunc TripleFlask, Nunclon Delta treated, straight neck, with its solid (non-vented) screw cap, cat. 132867 (about 11 US dollars each in a case of 32), clear polystyrene plastic with an HDPE plastic cap: a 205 mm long body, 147 mm wide and 56 mm thick (the T175 size), with a 30 mm neck 20 mm long and a 40 mm cap 25 mm long, centred on the neck end. Inside are three culture compartments, each 170 x 98 mm with a 13 mm gap, at a 15 mm pitch (500 cm2 in all); they are joined at the closed end by a slot above 7 mm lips, and at the neck end each opens over a 7 mm lip into the neck chamber, whose 28 mm bore leads to the cap. 0.25 kg empty (estimate), 0.45 kg filled. The Nunclon imprint is on the top face. Medium: 200 mL of tap water tinted with 10 drops of McCormick blue food colour, in place of a cell suspension. Start: the flask has been filled, capped tight, stood on its closed end so the compartments level, and rested on its long side. It lies on the table with its long axis along y and the cap toward the robot's right (cap centre at x 16.2, y -10 cm, 7.35 cm up), the top face toward the robot at x 13.4 cm and the bottom face at x 19 cm; the closed end is at y 13.75. Each compartment holds 66.7 mL, a 30.2 mm deep column on its side. Surfaces: friction 0.35 between the flask and the work surface and between the flask and the gripper pads (estimate). Both arms start in their ready pose. One fixed layout, zero object jitter. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Judged at the end of the run with a phone inclinometer or bubble level, a ruler, a 10 mL serological pipette on a pipette controller, a 100 mL graduated cylinder and the trial video. Layer volumes: after the trial the scorer opens the cap and, with the flask left flat, draws each layer dry through the neck with the pipette, its tip guided over the layer's lip through the clear wall (top, middle, bottom), into the cylinder, read to 1 mL; in the simulator they are the medium model's three volumes. Even: every layer within 60.0-73.3 mL (10% of 66.7 mL). Roughly even: every layer within 50.0-83.3 mL (25%). Flat: lying on its bottom face, imprint up, the top face within 5 degrees of level (inclinometer), resting on the table. Released and still: no gripper within 2 cm of the flask, and no point of it moving more than 1 mm over the last 3 s (video; a returning hand restarts the count). Score 0 if, at any time, even if it drains back: medium reaches the neck (more than 0.5 mL in the neck chamber; on the real bench any dye in the neck or cap thread), any corner of the flask reaches the table faster than 0.5 m/s (a splash into the neck; video frames), or the flask leaves the table (any point 1 cm below the table top). Otherwise, at the end, the first that fits: 1.0 flat, released and still, every layer even; 0.5 flat, released and still, every layer roughly even; 0.25 flat, released and still, some layer outside 50.0-83.3 mL; 0 anything else, including the untouched start (on its side), the flask imprint down, on its side or on end, still held or not still. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. The trial ends at the run limit or once 1.0 has held; only the end counts, except the zeros above. Standing it on end again, re-leaning or rolling more than once costs nothing.
run_limit: 1,200 steps (60 s at 20 Hz); the scripted one-hand demo reaches full score in about 16 s
reset_notes: Nothing is used up. After the layers are drawn off and read, pour the 200 mL back through the neck, cap it tight and wipe the neck; stand the flask on its closed end for 10 s so the compartments level, then rest it on its long side on the start marks (top face toward the robot, cap at y -10 cm) and wait 10 s; check with the level that it sits upright on its side. Replace the flask if dye stains the neck. Run the simulator with -E object_jitter=0 (one fixed layout).
fidelity: Rigid flask at real size, 0.45 kg with medium, mass spread by volume; cap and neck as 16 flats. The medium is an analytic model, no particles: three compartment volumes whose levels follow the flask's pose, joined at the closed end by a slot (2.5 mL/s per mm of level difference), kept apart flat by 7 mm lips. Medium over a neck-end lip, or a corner landing faster than 0.5 m/s, goes to the neck. Slot rate, lips and landing limit are estimates to check on a real flask. Nothing is moved by code.
